record.paper_title: Some open problems in random matrix theory and the theory of integrable systems
record.original_question: Develop a systematic and computationally reliable theory for the six Painlevé equations, analogous in spirit to the Bateman project or Abramowitz-Stegun for classical special functions. In particular, build dependable software and accompanying asymptotic and algebraic infrastructure for computing Painlevé transcendents, such as determining features like the pole locations in the complex plane for the Painlevé II solution asymptotic to the Airy function as x→+∞.

evidence.quote: What is needed is a project, similar to the Bateman project, or a new volume of Abramowitz and Stegun, devoted to the Painlevé equations.

If u(x) is the solution of the Painlevé II equation, say, which is asymptotic to the Airy function Ai(x) as x → +∞, one would like to know, for example, the location of its poles in the complex x-plane.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Develop a systematic and computationally reliable theory of the six Painlevé equations

  P_I:  u'' = 6u^2 + x,
  P_II: u'' = 2u^3 + xu + α,
  P_III, P_IV, P_V, P_VI (in their standard forms),

analogous in scope and reliability to classical handbooks of special functions (such as the Bateman Manuscript Project or the Abramowitz–Stegun Handbook). The goal is twofold:

(a) Produce dependable software and an accompanying asymptotic and algebraic infrastructure that, given any of the six Painlevé equations together with a choice of monodromy/Stokes data (or equivalently a choice of distinguished one-parameter family of solutions), reliably evaluates the corresponding Painlevé transcendent at arbitrary points of its domain, including connection formulas between asymptotic regimes and locations of movable singularities.

(b) As a concrete benchmark instance, for the Painlevé II equation
   u''(x) = 2u(x)^3 + x u(x)
let u(x) be the unique (Hastings–McLeod-type) real solution satisfying
   u(x) ∼ Ai(x) as x → +∞,
where Ai is the Airy function. Determine the locations in the complex x-plane of all poles of the meromorphic continuation of u, including their distribution, asymptotics, and an algorithm for computing them to prescribed accuracy.
artifact.status_search_result: The "Painlevé Project" envisioned as a community-wide handbook/software analogue of Bateman or Abramowitz–Stegun was formally launched at an ICMS workshop in Edinburgh (May 2010), with a coordinating site hosted at NIST and ongoing integration into the DLMF (chapter on Painlevé transcendents under revision). Substantial partial progress exists: numerical Riemann–Hilbert methods (Olver, Trogdon and others) reliably compute Painlevé II transcendents and their poles, and asymptotic/connection-formula knowledge for the tritronquée and Hastings–McLeod solutions has advanced. However, a complete, uniformly reliable handbook-plus-software covering all six Painlevé equations across all parameter regimes is still a work in progress rather than a finished product, so the broader programmatic problem remains partially solved.

status_evidence.title: The Painleve Project (NIST)
status_evidence.snippet: Coordinating e-site at NIST established as first step of the Painlevé Project, conceived at the ICMS Edinburgh workshop, May 10–14, 2010.
status_evidence.claim: A community Painlevé Project, analogous to Bateman/Abramowitz–Stegun, was formally initiated and is ongoing.

status_evidence.title: A Request: The Painlevé Project (Notices of the AMS, Dec. 2010)
status_evidence.snippet: Calls for organizing and tabulating algebraic, analytical, asymptotic and numerical properties of Painlevé functions, analogous to classical handbooks.
status_evidence.claim: The handbook-and-software programme is still being assembled by the community.

status_evidence.title: Numerical Solution of Riemann–Hilbert Problems: Painlevé II
status_evidence.snippet: Provides a numerical Riemann–Hilbert method that reliably evaluates Painlevé II transcendents, including pole locations.
status_evidence.claim: Reliable numerical evaluation of P_II solutions, including the Hastings–McLeod-type solution and its poles, has been partially achieved.
